paragraphs.text: A cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Menghai in Yunnan, pressed in 1996. The leaf was [fried in a wok and dried in the sun](sheng:making) and never hot-air dried. That leaves some of the leaf’s own activity alive, so the tea goes on changing for years after it is pressed.

At thirty years it sits well past the point where the trade starts to call raw pu’er [aged](sheng:ageing), whether that line is drawn at ten years or at twenty. How far any cake has come depends on where it was kept, because heat and humidity set the pace of its [change in storage](sheng:storage). This one was made in the decade when collectors, led at first by Taiwan, came looking for [aged raw pu’er](sheng:history-modern).

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
